title: Sorting waste: why we separate it the moment we throw it
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home today, in a city flat, with the materials listed. The two-jar test uses things every kitchen has: newspaper, a piece of a biscuit box, a rinsed milk packet, a peel and two spoons of leftover sambar or dal. Newspaper soaks up sambar within a few minutes, so the result is clear in a 15-minute wait. Wet newspaper tears with a gentle pull, while the dry strip from the other jar does not, so the child feels the difference in their own hands. The milk packet rinses clean under the tap, which surprises most children and is a real result: plastic, metal and glass can be washed, paper and cloth cannot. The next-day smell check is optional and is done near a window by a grown-up. The sorting race uses 30 small things from the kitchen and the dustbin, and the mixed round really takes several times longer, because used tea leaves stick to paper. Gloves or a spoon are used for the mixed round. The lid test depends on ants or fruit flies finding the open box. They nearly always do in a warm Indian kitchen within a day, and the step says what to do if they don't. The building walk and the poster project are outside the core path, because not every family can go round their building. Both games were checked to finish.

summary.text: A dry newspaper can be sold, pulped and made into new paper. Drop it in a bin with wet sambar and peels, and within minutes it is soaked, stained and tears in your hand. No washing can make it good paper again. That is why we sort waste the moment we throw it: wet waste in one bin, dry waste in another, and dangerous things like batteries, tube lights and broken glass in a box of their own. You will soak waste in two jars, race to sort waste before and after it is mixed, and set up a sorting station at home.
summary.art: Two glass jars side by side on a kitchen counter. In the left jar, a crisp newspaper strip, a biscuit-box piece and a milk packet sit clean and dry. In the right jar, the same three things lie in sambar, rice and a banana peel, the newspaper dark and soggy. Behind them, a green bin, a blue bin and a small red-marked box.

intro.hook: Take one sheet of newspaper and tear it in half. Dip one half in a bowl of water for a minute. Now pull each half gently from both ends. Which one tears first?
intro.text: Every home in India throws out two very different kinds of waste. Wet waste is food and other things that rot, like peels, leftover rice and used tea leaves. Dry waste is things that do not rot quickly, like paper, plastic, metal and glass. Dry waste that is clean can be sold and made into new things. But when the two kinds go into one bag, the wet soaks into the dry. Can we ever separate them again afterwards? The two-jar test will show you.
intro.art: A child pulling two halves of a newspaper sheet, one dry and whole, one wet and tearing in the middle, over a steel bowl of water.

outcomes: I can say what wet waste, dry waste and household hazardous waste are, and put everyday things in the right bin.
I can run a fair test to show what happens to dry waste when wet waste is mixed with it.
I can explain why sorting is easiest at the moment we throw something, and much harder once things are mixed.
I can name dangerous waste at home, like batteries, tube lights, medicines and broken glass, and say how to keep it safe for the people who collect it.
I can explain how open bins, garbage heaps and standing water make a home or a lane unsafe, and what keeps them clean.
I can name the people who collect and sort our waste, and say how sorting at home makes their work safer.

terms.meaning: Anything we have finished using and throw out.
terms.example: Onion peels, an empty toothpaste tube and yesterday's newspaper are all waste.
terms.art: A kitchen counter with an onion peel, an empty toothpaste tube and a folded newspaper.

terms.meaning: Waste that rots, because tiny living things can feed on it. Most of it is food.
terms.example: Vegetable peels, leftover rice, used tea leaves, eggshells and old flowers.
terms.art: A green bin holding vegetable peels, tea leaves, eggshells and a wilted flower garland.

terms.meaning: Waste that does not rot quickly, like paper, plastic, metal, glass and cloth. When clean, much of it can be recycled.
terms.example: A rinsed milk packet, a cardboard box, a steel lid, a glass jar and an old cotton rag.
terms.art: A blue bin holding a flattened cardboard box, a rinsed milk packet, a glass jar and a tin lid.

terms.meaning: Waste from home that can hurt people, animals or the soil if it is thrown out with the rest. Hazardous means dangerous.
terms.example: Old batteries, broken tube lights, broken glass, used blades, old medicines and paint tins.
terms.art: A small cardboard box marked with a red cross, holding a few used batteries, a wrapped tube light and a strip of old tablets.

terms.meaning: Putting each kind of waste in its own bin or bag. People also call this segregating waste.
terms.example: Peels go in the green bin, the milk packet goes in the blue bin, and the battery goes in the danger box.
terms.art: A child dropping a peel in a green bin and a milk packet in a blue bin.

terms.meaning: Sorting waste in the place where it is made, like your kitchen, before anything is mixed.
terms.example: Sorting in the kitchen is sorting at source. Sorting at a garbage dump is not.
terms.art: A kitchen with three bins under the counter, and an arrow showing a hand dropping things in the right one.

terms.meaning: Wet, dry and dangerous waste thrown together in one bag or bin.
terms.example: One plastic bag holding sambar, newspaper, a battery and a broken glass.
terms.art: A torn plastic bag with sambar leaking out over newspaper, a battery and broken glass.

terms.meaning: To break used paper, plastic, metal or glass down into raw material and make new things from it.
terms.example: Old newspapers are soaked into pulp at a paper mill and made into new paper.
terms.art: A pile of newspapers going into a mill, and a fresh roll of paper coming out.

terms.meaning: To make something dirty or unsafe by mixing something else into it.
terms.example: Sambar soaking into newspaper contaminates the paper, so it can no longer be recycled.
terms.art: A crisp newspaper strip beside the same strip stained orange with sambar.

terms.meaning: To soak up a liquid into the inside of something.
terms.example: Paper, cardboard and cotton absorb sambar. A plastic packet does not, so it can be rinsed.
terms.art: A drop of sambar spreading into a newspaper, and the same drop sitting as a bead on a milk packet.

terms.meaning: A place where a city dumps its waste in a huge heap and covers it with soil.
terms.example: Brahmapuram near Kochi and Deonar in Mumbai are big dumping grounds.
terms.art: A tall heap of garbage outside a city, with crows and kites circling above it.

terms.meaning: A person who collects and sorts waste and sells what can be recycled. Many are women.
terms.example: In Kerala, women of the Haritha Karma Sena collect sorted dry waste from homes.
terms.art: Two women in green uniforms sorting sacks of dry waste in a collection shed.

terms.meaning: A silvery metal that is liquid at room temperature. It is poisonous to people and animals.
terms.example: Tube lights and the curly CFL bulbs hold a tiny amount of mercury. This is why they go in the danger box.
terms.art: A silvery drop of mercury on a dish, beside a tube light and a curly bulb.

terms.meaning: To have young. Mosquitoes breed by laying eggs in still water.
terms.example: Rain water caught in a thrown-away coconut shell or cup is a place where mosquitoes breed.
terms.art: A coconut shell holding rainwater, with tiny mosquito young wriggling in it.

explanations.definition: Household waste is sorted into three kinds: wet waste, which rots; dry waste, which does not rot quickly; and household hazardous waste, which is dangerous.
explanations.description: Wet waste is mostly food: peels, leftovers, tea leaves, eggshells and old flowers. Tiny living things like bacteria and fungi feed on wet waste. They turn it into compost. Dry waste is paper, plastic, metal, glass, rubber and cloth. When it is clean and dry, much of it can be recycled. Hazardous waste can hurt people or the soil, like batteries, tube lights, medicines, blades and broken glass. India's Solid Waste Management Rules of 2016 ask every home to keep these three kinds apart. Many cities use a green bin for wet waste and a blue bin for dry waste.
examples: Wet: a banana peel, leftover rice, used coffee powder from the filter.
Dry: a rinsed milk packet, a cardboard box, a steel lid.
Hazardous: an old battery, a broken tube light, a strip of expired tablets.
explanations.art: Three containers in a row: a green bin with peels, a blue bin with paper and a milk packet, and a small box with a red cross holding a battery and a wrapped tube light.

explanations.definition: Paper, cardboard and cloth absorb liquids from wet waste. Once soaked and stained, they cannot be recycled into good new material.
explanations.description: Paper is made of tiny plant fibres pressed together. Liquid gets in between the fibres and loosens them, so wet paper tears easily. Oil and food stuck in paper cannot be washed out at the paper mill, and they spoil the new paper. So the mill does not take it. Plastic, metal and glass do not absorb liquid. Their surface gets dirty, but they can be rinsed. So mixing hurts paper and cloth most. Mixed waste also smells, draws flies and rats, and is unsafe for the people who sort it.
examples: A dry newspaper can be sold to the kabadiwala. A newspaper soaked in sambar cannot.
A pizza box with cheese stuck on it is not taken for recycling. A clean cardboard box is.
A milk packet smeared with curd can be rinsed and dried, and then it is dry waste again.
explanations.art: A close-up drawing of paper fibres like a tangle of threads, with liquid seeping between them, next to a smooth plastic surface where the liquid sits on top.

explanations.concept: Mixing is quick, unmixing is slow
explanations.definition: Things mix by themselves the moment they touch. Separating them again always takes work and time, and sometimes it cannot be done.
explanations.description: Drop a newspaper into sambar and the sambar soaks in without anyone doing anything. Getting the sambar out again is not possible. Even things that do not soak in get stuck together. Tea leaves cling to paper, and broken glass hides in peels. So a heap of mixed waste takes many hours of hand sorting, and much of it is never sorted at all. Scientists see this everywhere in nature: sugar spreads through tea by itself, but never gathers back into a lump. It is always easier to keep things apart than to pull them apart.
examples: A drop of ink spreads through a glass of water by itself. Nobody can pull it back into a drop.
In the sorting race, sorting 30 things into bins as you throw them is quick. Sorting the same 30 after they are mixed with wet tea leaves takes much longer.
Waste pickers at dumping grounds spend their whole day pulling dry waste out of mixed heaps.
explanations.art: A glass of water with a drop of ink spreading out in curls, and beside it a hand trying to pick tea leaves off a wet newspaper.

explanations.concept: What happens to sorted waste and to mixed waste
explanations.definition: Sorted wet waste can become compost or cooking gas, and sorted dry waste can be recycled. Mixed waste mostly ends up on a dump.
explanations.description: Sorted wet waste can go to a compost pot at home, or to a city compost yard or biogas plant. Bacteria make biogas from wet waste. Biogas is a gas that can be used for cooking. Sorted dry waste goes to a kabadiwala or a dry waste collection centre. There, people sort it again into paper, hard plastic, soft plastic, metal and glass, and sell each kind. Mixed waste is hard to use. Most of it is dumped on a landfill. In a landfill, the wet waste rots without air and makes methane, a gas that warms the Earth and catches fire easily. In March 2023, the dumping ground at Brahmapuram near Kochi caught fire, and smoke covered parts of the city for nearly two weeks.
examples: Peels from a sorted green bin become compost for a balcony plant.
Clean newspapers from a sorted blue bin are sold by weight to the kabadiwala.
A bag of mixed waste goes to the dumping ground, where it can rot, smell and burn.
explanations.art: Three paths from a home: a green bin to a compost pot with a plant growing, a blue bin to a kabadiwala's cart and a paper mill, and a mixed bag to a smoking garbage mountain.

explanations.concept: Dangerous waste needs its own box
explanations.definition: Household hazardous waste is kept apart, wrapped and marked, because it can cut, poison or burn the people and animals who touch it later.
explanations.description: Broken glass and used blades cut the hands of the people who sort waste, so wrap them in thick newspaper and write 'broken glass' on it. Tube lights and curly CFL bulbs hold a tiny amount of mercury, a poisonous metal, so do not break them. Phone and laptop batteries can catch fire when they are crushed in a garbage truck. Old medicines should never be flushed or thrown loose, because they can harm animals that eat them and get into water. Used diapers and sanitary pads are wrapped in newspaper and marked, so that nobody opens them. Keep a small box for dangerous waste, and ask your city or a shop that sells batteries or bulbs where it can be taken.
examples: A broken glass tumbler wrapped in newspaper and marked 'broken glass'.
Old batteries kept in a jar until there are enough to take to a collection point.
A box of expired tablets kept aside, not thrown in the bin.
explanations.art: A child's hands wrapping a broken tumbler in thick newspaper, and a grown-up writing 'BROKEN GLASS' on it with a marker.

explanations.concept: How waste makes a home or lane unsafe
explanations.definition: Open waste draws flies, rats, crows and stray animals, and thrown-away containers catch rainwater where mosquitoes breed.
explanations.description: Food in an open bin smells, and flies, cockroaches and rats come to feed. Flies walk on the waste and then on our food, carrying germs. Animals tear open garbage bags on the road and scatter the waste further. Cows and dogs may swallow plastic bags with food in them. After rain, a thrown-away cup, tyre or coconut shell holds still water. Mosquitoes breed in it, and some of them spread dengue. Plastic bags block drains, so water floods the street. A bin with a lid, waste taken out every day, and nothing left where water can collect keep a home and a lane safe.
examples: A coconut shell left on a terrace after rain can hold mosquito young within a week.
A bin with a lid keeps flies and ants out of the kitchen.
A drain blocked by plastic bags floods the road after a heavy shower.
explanations.art: A lane after rain: an overflowing open bin with flies and a crow, a coconut shell full of water, and a drain choked with plastic bags. Beside it, a clean doorstep with a closed bin.

explanations.concept: The people who handle our waste
explanations.definition: Collectors, waste pickers, kabadiwalas and sanitation workers carry, sort and sell our waste. Sorting at home makes their work cleaner, safer and better paid.
explanations.description: Every bag a home throws out is touched again by somebody's hands. In many cities, waste pickers sort dry waste and sell it, and many of them are women. In Kerala, women of the Haritha Karma Sena go from home to home collecting sorted dry waste. In Pune, waste pickers formed a group called SWaCH to collect waste from homes. When waste arrives sorted, clean paper and plastic sell for more, and nobody is cut by hidden glass. For a long time in India, cleaning other people's waste was pushed onto certain castes. Taking charge of our own waste is also about fairness.
examples: A collector can sell a bundle of clean, dry newspaper. A soaked bundle is worth nothing.
A waste picker sorting a mixed bag can be cut by a blade hidden inside.
A thank-you and a sorted bag make a waste collector's day easier.
explanations.art: A woman in a green uniform at a building gate, receiving a blue bag of dry waste from a child, with a cart of sorted sacks behind her.

explanations.concept: Whether every home should sort, or machines should do it
explanations.description: Nearly everyone agrees that sorted waste is easier to use. People disagree about who should do the sorting.

perspectives.who: Most waste experts, and India's 2016 rules
perspectives.explanation: Sort at source. Mixing happens in seconds and cannot be undone, so the person holding the waste is the best one to sort it. It costs almost nothing at home.
Families make mistakes and many will never sort. Big sorting plants with belts, magnets, blowers and trained workers can separate dry waste on a large scale.
Homes should sort, and the waste should go to the waste pickers who already know the work, not to big plants that take away their living.

examples: Bengaluru and Indore ask every home to hand over waste sorted.
Some cities run sorting plants that pull out metal with magnets.
Even a sorting plant cannot take sambar back out of a newspaper.
explanations.art: Three speech bubbles over a city: a family sorting at home, an engineer at a sorting machine with a moving belt, and a waste picker with sacks.

agreed.text: Clean, dry paper, plastic, metal and glass can be recycled. Paper soaked or stained with food usually cannot.
agreed.evidence: Paper mills reject paper with food and oil on it, because these spoil the new paper. You can feel the difference yourself: soaked newspaper tears with a gentle pull.

agreed.text: Sorting waste at home, before it is mixed, is the easiest and cheapest way to sort it.
agreed.evidence: Cities that collect waste already sorted, like Indore and Mysuru, recover far more compost and recyclable material. Sorting a mixed heap by hand is slow, dirty and dangerous.

agreed.text: Wet waste dumped in heaps makes methane, a gas that warms the Earth and catches fire.
agreed.evidence: Gas is measured coming out of landfills all over the world. Dumping grounds like Deonar in Mumbai and Brahmapuram near Kochi have had large fires.

agreed.text: Still water in thrown-away containers lets mosquitoes breed, and some of them spread dengue.
agreed.evidence: Health workers find mosquito young in coconut shells, cups, tyres and pots after rain. Clearing these is one of the main ways cities fight dengue.

agreed.text: Poisonous waste does not become safe by being spread out in water.
agreed.evidence: At Minamata in Japan, mercury poured into the sea built up in fish and made people and cats very ill. This is why mercury and other dangerous waste are kept apart.

challenging.claim: There is no point sorting at home, because the truck mixes it all again.
challenging.for: In some places this really happened. Workers tipped sorted bags into one truck, and people stopped bothering.
challenging.against: Most cities now collect wet and dry waste in separate parts of the truck or on separate days. Where they don't, the fix is to complain, not to stop sorting. Once mixed at home, the dry waste is already spoiled.
challenging.context: Some families say sorting is useless. This card asks whether that is true.

challenging.claim: Waste-to-energy plants can burn mixed waste, so we don't need to sort.
challenging.for: Burning waste in a closed plant can make electricity. Burning also shrinks the heap.
challenging.against: Indian waste is about half wet food, which is full of water and burns badly. Several such plants in India have struggled and been blamed for smoke. Burning also destroys paper and plastic that could have been recycled.
challenging.context: Some people say we can burn our waste for electricity instead of sorting it. This card weighs that up.

challenging.claim: Composting is only for houses with gardens.
challenging.for: A compost heap in a garden is the usual picture of composting.
challenging.against: Wet waste can be composted in clay pots stacked on a balcony, or in a closed bucket with holes. Many apartment buildings in Bengaluru and Chennai run their own compost units.
challenging.context: People in flats often think composting is not for them. This card checks.

challenging.claim: Poisonous waste poured into the sea is safe, because the sea is so big.
challenging.who: Many factories and officials until the 1960s
challenging.for: A small amount of poison spread through a huge amount of water is very weak.
challenging.against: Tiny living things in the water take up the mercury. Small fish eat them, and big fish eat many small fish, so the mercury builds up. At Minamata, people and cats who ate the fish became very ill.
challenging.context: People once thought the sea could take any waste. This card is about why that was wrong.

challenging.claim: Plastic is always the worst kind of waste.
challenging.for: Plastic lasts for a very long time, spreads into seas and soil, and animals swallow it.
challenging.against: Some dangerous waste, like mercury, batteries and medicines, is far more harmful in small amounts. And wet waste, when mixed and dumped, makes methane and fires. Each kind of waste has its own harm.
challenging.context: Plastic is often called the worst waste. This card asks whether one kind is always worst.

big_questions.q: If mixing takes one second and unmixing takes hours, whose job should sorting be?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is holding the waste at the moment it is easiest to sort.

big_questions.q: Why does sambar soak into newspaper but sit on top of a milk packet?
big_questions.hint: Think about what paper is made of. Look at a torn edge of newspaper closely.

big_questions.q: Why does sugar spread through tea by itself, but never gather back into a lump?
big_questions.hint: There are many more ways for the sugar to be spread out than to be in one lump.

big_questions.q: When you put a bag outside your door, who touches it next? And after them?
big_questions.hint: Follow the bag in your mind, from your door to the place it ends up.

big_questions.q: Is a thing still 'yours' after you throw it out?
big_questions.hint: Think of the mercury at Minamata. Who did the harm belong to?

big_questions.q: Could a city have no garbage heaps at all?
big_questions.hint: Think of what would have to happen in every home, every day.

story.title: Lissy Chechi Says No
story.note: The Brahmapuram fire is real. In March 2023 the dumping ground at Brahmapuram, near Kochi, burned for nearly two weeks, and smoke covered parts of the city. The Haritha Karma Sena is real too: groups of women in Kerala's towns and villages who collect sorted dry waste from homes. Nila, her uncle Babu, Lissy chechi and what they say are made up.
text: The smoke came on a Thursday. Nila woke up in her flat in Kochi and the sky outside the window was grey, though there were no clouds. The air smelled like burnt rubber. Her mother shut all the windows and stuffed a towel under the balcony door.
'The Brahmapuram dump is on fire,' her mother said, reading her phone. 'They say it may burn for days.'

Nila's uncle Babu was staying with them that week. He had come from the Gulf, where he worked, and he liked to cook. That evening he made fish curry and appam for everyone. Afterwards he cleared up. He scraped the plates into a big plastic bag. In went the fish bones and the leftover curry. In went the newspaper he had used to drain the fried fish, the empty milk packets, a broken glass and the curry powder box. Last of all, he dropped in the old torch battery from the drawer. He tied the bag in a knot and set it by the front door.
'Babu Mama,' said Nila. 'Lissy chechi won't take that.'
'Who is Lissy chechi?' he asked.
'She collects our waste. You'll see.'

Lissy chechi came the next morning in her green uniform, with a face mask over her nose because of the smoke. She worked for the Haritha Karma Sena, a group of women who collected dry waste from every flat in the building. She looked at the knotted bag by the door. She lifted it a little, and something dripped onto the floor.
'Sorry, mone,' she said to Uncle Babu, kindly but firmly. 'I can't take this one. It's mixed.'
Uncle Babu laughed. 'It's all rubbish, chechi. What does it matter how it's packed?'
Lissy chechi put down her sack. 'Can I show you?' she asked. She opened the bag on an old sheet of newspaper on the landing, with her gloves on. Nila crouched beside her.

Lissy chechi picked up the newspaper that had drained the fish. It was orange and soaked through. When she lifted it by one corner, it tore and fell back into the curry. 'Dry, this paper is money,' she said. 'The kabadi shop buys it by the kilo, and the mill makes new paper from it. Soaked in curry, it is nothing. Nobody can wash curry out of paper.'

Next she picked up a milk packet. It was smeared with curry, but when Nila rinsed it under the tap on the landing, it came clean. 'This one can be saved,' said Lissy chechi. 'Plastic doesn't drink the curry. Paper does.'

Then she stopped. Very carefully, she pulled out the pieces of the broken glass, one by one, and laid them on the paper. 'If I had put my hand in without looking,' she said quietly. Uncle Babu stopped smiling.
Last, she held up the torch battery. 'And this should never go in any bag. Batteries can leak or catch fire. Keep them in a jar until we take them to the collection point.'
Uncle Babu looked at the heap on the landing. 'I'm sorry, chechi,' he said. 'It took me one minute to put all that in one bag.'

'That's the trouble,' said Lissy chechi. 'It takes one minute to mix. It takes a person all day to pull a mixed heap apart, and most of it never gets pulled apart at all.' She pointed through the stairwell window, at the grey sky. 'Where do you think the mixed bags go?'
Nila looked at the smoke. 'To Brahmapuram,' she said.

'A mountain of mixed bags,' said Lissy chechi. 'The food rots inside it and makes a gas that burns. The plastic and paper are stuck in the rotting food, so nobody can take them out. And then one day it catches fire.'

That afternoon, Nila set up the kitchen. She put a steel bucket with a lid under the sink for wet waste and wrote WET on it. She put a cardboard box beside it for dry waste and wrote DRY. She found an old biscuit tin for the danger box and drew a red cross on the lid. She wrapped the broken glass in three sheets of newspaper and wrote BROKEN GLASS on it in big letters. Then she taught Uncle Babu. 'Fish bones, wet. Milk packet, rinse it, then dry. Newspaper, dry, but only if it's clean. Battery, the tin.'
Uncle Babu tried it all week. On Wednesday he forgot and put a tea bag in the dry box. Nila fished it out with a spoon. One tea bag had made a brown stain on a whole stack of newspapers.
'One second of carelessness,' said Uncle Babu, looking at the stain. 'And no way to undo it.'

On Friday, Lissy chechi came again. Uncle Babu was waiting at the door with a bag of clean, dry newspapers, a bundle of rinsed milk packets and a cardboard box folded flat. 'Sorted, chechi,' he said. 'And this time, I sorted it myself.'

Lissy chechi weighed the paper on her hanging scale and smiled. 'Now this,' she said, 'is worth something.' The rain came that night and the smoke over Kochi began to clear. In the kitchen, the green bucket was full of peels for the compost pot, and the blue box was full of things that would be made new.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Lissy chechi says it takes one minute to mix and all day to pull apart. Uncle Babu thinks waste is one thing, 'all rubbish'. Lissy chechi shows him that what was dry paper and money became curry-soaked rubbish only because it was put in the same bag. The tea bag on Wednesday makes the same point in a small way: mixing happens instantly and cannot be undone. The story also shows who really carries the risk of mixed waste: the hidden glass would have cut Lissy chechi, not Uncle Babu.
ask: Uncle Babu said, 'It's all rubbish. What does it matter how it's packed?' What did Lissy chechi show him?
Why could the milk packet be saved, but not the newspaper?
Who would have been hurt by the broken glass in the mixed bag?
How was the fire at the dump connected to bags like Uncle Babu's?
One tea bag stained a whole stack of newspapers. What does that tell you about where sorting should happen?
