games.title: Three Bins Snap

setup.art: Three paper mats on the floor marked WET in green, DRY in blue and DANGER with a red cross, and a pile of face-down cards.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three bin mats and the shuffled cards.

setup.art: A girl turning over a card showing a banana peel while two children race to slap the green WET mat.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card and race to slap the right mat.

games.context: This is a fast card game. A card is turned over showing a thing people throw out, and players race to slap the right bin mat: WET, DRY or DANGER.

printables.title: 30 waste cards to cut out
items: A paint tin with paint left in it
TRICKY: a newspaper soaked in sambar
TRICKY: a pizza box with cheese stuck on it
TRICKY: a curd cup with curd still inside

printables.title: Three bin mats
items: DRY (blue): clean paper, plastic, metal, glass, cloth
DANGER (red cross): it can cut, poison or burn

rules: Lay the three mats in the middle, where everyone can reach them.
Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top card and reads it aloud.
Everyone races to slap the right mat. The first correct slap wins the card.
A wrong slap means you miss the next card.
On a TRICKY card, the first player to slap must also explain their choice. A good explanation wins 2 cards.
When the pile is empty, the player with the most cards wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and mats. 2. Lay out the three mats. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Each card is something we throw out. Slap the bin it belongs in, as fast as you can.
flow.kid: Each card is some waste. Slap the right bin, fast!
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Bins Snap, a card game about sorting waste.

flow.do: Play through the pile. Stop on each TRICKY card and talk it over.
flow.say: This one is tricky. Where does it go, and why?
flow.kid: Play the cards. On a TRICKY card, say why you chose that bin.
flow.parent: TRICKY answers: the soaked newspaper is now wet or reject waste, not dry, because it can't be recycled. The tea bag goes in WET. The pizza box: tear off the clean part for DRY, and the cheesy part goes in WET. The curd cup: scrape and rinse it, then DRY. The broken CFL bulb: DANGER, wrapped, because it has mercury.

flow.do: Count the cards and talk about the hardest one.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which card was hardest?

check.q: In Three Bins Snap, where does the newspaper soaked in sambar go?
options: DRY, because newspaper is always dry waste
WET, because it is soaked with food and can no longer be recycled
check.why: Clean newspaper is dry waste. But once it is soaked with sambar, the paper mill can't use it. It rots along with the food, so it goes with wet waste. That is why we keep newspaper away from food in the first place.

games.title: Mix-Up Memory

setup.art: 24 small cards laid face down in rows on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 24 cards face down in rows.

setup.art: A child turning over two cards, 'Clean newspaper' and 'Sold by the kilo and made into new paper', and smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. A thing and what happens to it make a pair.

games.context: This is a memory game about what happens when waste is mixed. Each pair is a thing and what happens to it when it is mixed or sorted.

printables.title: 24 cards: 12 pairs to cut out
items: Sold by the kilo and made into new paper
Tears apart and can't be recycled
Peels kept in the wet bin
Peels in a plastic bag on the dump
Rot without air and make methane, a gas that burns
Broken glass hidden in a mixed bag
A coconut shell left out in the rain

rules: Shuffle the cards and lay them face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over two cards.
If they are a thing and what happens to it, say why, and keep them. Then take another turn.
If not, turn them back over. The next player goes.
When all pairs are found, the player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns it takes to find all 12 pairs, and try to beat it next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards, shuffle them and lay them face down.
flow.say: Each pair is a thing and what happens to it. Find the pairs.
flow.kid: Find a thing and what happens to it. That is a pair.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mix-Up Memory, a memory game about sorted and mixed waste.

flow.do: Play until all pairs are found. Ask for the reason each time.
flow.say: Why does that happen to it? Tell me before you keep the pair.
flow.kid: Turn two cards. If they match, say why.
flow.parent: Listen for reasons from the unit: paper soaks up liquid, rotting without air makes methane, mosquitoes breed in still water.

flow.do: Look at all the pairs together and sort them into 'sorted' and 'mixed'.
flow.say: Which pairs show sorted waste? Which show mixed waste? Which pile has the happier endings?
flow.kid: Put the sorted pairs in one pile, mixed in another. Which pile ends better?

check.q: In Mix-Up Memory, peels kept in the wet bin become compost, but peels in a plastic bag on the dump make methane. Why the difference?
options: On the dump they are shut in plastic and buried, so they rot without air
check.why: Peels rotting with air become compost. Shut in plastic deep in a dump, they rot without air, and the tiny living things that do that kind of rotting give off methane. The peels are the same. Where they end up is different.

items.p: Sort these things into wet waste and dry waste.
items.a: see items
items.why: Wet waste is food and other things that rot. Dry waste is paper, plastic, metal, glass and cloth, which do not rot quickly.

items.p: Which of these is household hazardous waste?
items.why: Batteries can leak harmful metals or catch fire, so they go in the danger box. A peel is wet waste. A newspaper and a rag are dry waste.

items.p: Sorting waste in the kitchen, before it is mixed, is called sorting at ____.
items.why: The source is the place where the waste is made. Sorting there is easiest, because nothing is mixed yet.

items.p: A newspaper soaked in sambar can be washed and then sold for recycling.
items.why: False. Paper absorbs the sambar between its fibres. Washing makes it fall apart. That is why it must be kept away from wet waste.

items.p: A plastic milk packet with a little curd on it can be rinsed and put in the dry bin.
items.why: True. Plastic does not absorb liquid, so a quick rinse cleans it. In the Two-Jar Test, the milk packet came clean.

items.p: Match each thing to where it goes.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Peels rot, so they are wet. Glass and clean paper are dry. A tube light holds mercury, a poison, so it goes in the danger box.

items.p: In the Two-Jar Test, what happened to the newspaper strip in the jar with sambar?
opts: It soaked up the sambar and tore when pulled
items.why: Paper is made of plant fibres with gaps between them. The sambar soaked into the gaps, the fibres came loose, and the strip tore.
items.context: In the Two-Jar Test, you put the same newspaper, biscuit-box piece and milk packet in two jars, and added sambar and peels to one jar.

items.p: Three of these are wet waste. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Coconut, jasmine flowers and curry leaves all come from plants and rot. A plastic straw does not rot, so it is dry waste.

items.p: Why should a kitchen wet bin have a lid?
opts: To keep smells in and keep ants and flies out
items.why: Ants and flies find food by smell. A lid keeps most of the smell in and blocks the way in, as the Lid or No Lid test showed.

items.p: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still ____, like rain caught in a thrown-away cup.
items.why: Mosquito young grow in still water for about a week. Emptying cups, tyres and coconut shells stops them.

items.p: Write WET, DRY or DANGER on the label under each of the three containers.
items.why: The bin with peels and tea leaves is WET, the one with paper and packets is DRY, and the tin with batteries and a wrapped bulb is DANGER.
items.art: Three containers in a row with blank labels: a bucket with peels and tea leaves, a box with newspapers and a milk packet, and a small tin with batteries and a wrapped tube light.

items.p: In your own words, why do we keep wet waste away from dry waste?
items.a: Wet waste soaks into paper and cardboard and spoils them. Then they cannot be recycled. Mixed waste also smells and draws flies.
items.why: A strong answer says what wet waste does to dry waste and why that matters, ideally using the Two-Jar Test as evidence.

items.p: Draw your sorting station at home. Draw two things that go in each container.
items.a: A drawing of three containers labelled wet, dry and danger, each with two correct things, like peels and tea leaves, a newspaper and a bottle, a battery and tablets.
items.why: Drawing the station helps you remember it. Any correct things are right.

items.p: Name one person who handles your waste after it leaves your home. How does sorting help them?
items.a: Our waste collector. Sorting means she doesn't get cut by hidden glass, and she can sell clean paper and plastic.
items.why: A strong answer names a real person or job and gives a clear way sorting helps, like safety or being able to sell clean waste.

items.p: Where should broken glass go?
opts: Wrapped in thick newspaper, marked 'broken glass', and kept apart
In the wet bin, under the peels
items.why: Wrapping and marking warns the next person, so nobody is cut. Hiding it under peels is the most dangerous choice, because nobody can see it.

items.p: In the Two-Jar Test, the milk packet from the sambar jar came clean when rinsed, but the biscuit-box piece stayed stained. What explains this?
opts: Cardboard is made of paper fibres that absorb liquid, and plastic is not
The milk packet was rinsed for longer
items.why: Cardboard is pressed paper fibres, so liquid soaks in. Plastic has no gaps, so liquid stays on the surface. Picking 'rinsed for longer' would mean the test was unfair, but both were rinsed for ten seconds.
items.context: In the Two-Jar Test, you put the same newspaper, biscuit-box piece and milk packet in two jars, and added sambar and peels to one jar.

items.p: Your guess before the Two-Jar Test, and what happened. Were you right? What did the test teach you that the guess did not?
items.a: I guessed everything could be washed. But the newspaper tore and the box piece stayed stained. Only the milk packet came clean. So paper can't be saved once it is soaked.
items.why: A strong answer compares the guess and the result honestly, and says what was learned. Being wrong in a guess is how scientists learn.
items.context: In the Two-Jar Test, you put the same newspaper, biscuit-box piece and milk packet in two jars, and added sambar and peels to one jar.

items.p: In the Sorting Race, Round 1 took 40 seconds. Round 2, with mixed waste, took 200 seconds. How many times longer did Round 2 take?
items.why: 200 divided by 40 is 5. So sorting the mixed waste took 5 times as long. You can check: 40 + 40 + 40 + 40 + 40 = 200.
items.context: In the Sorting Race, you timed sorting 30 things as they were handed to you, and then sorting the same 30 after they were mixed with wet tea leaves.

items.p: Why does a heap of mixed waste on a dumping ground sometimes catch fire?
opts: Food rotting deep inside, without air, makes methane, a gas that burns
items.why: Deep in a heap, food rots without air and the tiny living things doing it give off methane. Methane burns easily. Once a fire starts, the plastic and paper burn too.

items.p: Waste that is poisonous becomes safe if you pour it into a big sea, because it spreads out.
items.why: False. At Minamata in Japan, mercury poured into the sea was taken up by tiny living things, then fish, and built up instead of spreading out. People and cats who ate the fish were poisoned.

items.p: Three people argue about who should sort a city's waste.

views.who: Priya, a mother in a Chennai flat
views.says: Every home should sort its own waste. It takes a few seconds at the bin.
Families make too many mistakes. Big sorting plants with machines can do it better.
Homes should sort, and the waste should come to people like me. This is our living.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason from your own tests. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence, for example that in the Two-Jar Test the paper was spoiled within 15 minutes, so no sorting plant could save the paper later. It then fairly says what another view gets right, like that machines can sort metal quickly.
items.why: Each view has some truth. The Two-Jar Test supports sorting at home, because mixing does harm before any plant sees the waste.

items.p: Put these in order, from what happens first to what happens last, for a bag of sorted dry waste.
items: You rinse the milk packet and put it in the dry box
The collector takes the dry bag
Workers at a collection centre sort it into paper, plastic and metal
A factory melts the plastic and makes something new
items.a: order shown
items.why: Dry waste moves from home, to the collector, to a sorting centre, and then to factories that recycle each material.

items.p: Fathima's family puts their peels inside a plastic bag and then into the wet bin. What is the problem?
opts: The plastic bag won't rot, so it spoils the compost
The bag makes the peels dry
items.why: Compost is made from things that rot. A plastic bag stays in the compost as plastic pieces. Peels can go into the wet bin loose, or wrapped in newspaper.

items.p: Is each of these a danger to people, or a danger to the soil and water, or both?
items.a: see items
items.why: A blade cuts hands. Medicines that get into water harm fish. A broken tube light has sharp glass and mercury. A leaking battery can burn skin and its metals can reach soil.

items.p: Your friend says, 'There is no point sorting, because the truck mixes it all again.' What would you say to her?
items.a: If we mix at home, the paper is already spoiled, like in my Two-Jar Test. Many trucks have separate parts. If ours doesn't, we should tell the city, not stop sorting.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the unit and suggests a fix, instead of only disagreeing.

items.p: Match each problem to how it is fixed.
pairs: Empty it and turn it over
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each fix stops the harm where it starts: lids keep flies out, empty shells hold no water for mosquitoes, wrapping warns people, and loose peels make clean compost.

items.p: Draw two paths for a piece of newspaper: one if it goes in the dry bin, and one if it goes in a mixed bag.
items.a: One path from a dry bin to a kabadiwala, a paper mill and new paper. Another from a mixed bag to a dumping ground, where it rots or burns.
items.why: The same newspaper ends up in very different places depending on what it is thrown with.

items.p: The poisonous metal inside a tube light is called ____.
items.why: Tube lights and curly CFL bulbs hold a tiny amount of mercury. It stays sealed if the tube is kept whole.

items.p: Asha throws a used tea bag into the dry box, onto a stack of newspapers. What is the most likely result?
opts: A brown stain spreads into the newspapers below it
The tea bag dries and turns into paper
The newspapers turn into compost straight away
items.why: The wet tea bag leaks tea, and the paper absorbs it. One wet thing can spoil many dry things beneath it. Tea bags go in the wet bin.

items.p: About half of the waste Indian homes throw out is wet waste.
items.why: True. Studies of Indian city waste find that roughly half is food and other things that rot. That is why composting wet waste makes such a big difference.

items.p: Sugar stirred into tea spreads out by itself, but it never gathers back into a lump. How is this like mixed waste?
items.a: Things mix by themselves when they touch, like sambar soaking into paper. Getting them apart again needs a lot of work, or can't be done. So it is easier to keep them apart from the start.
items.why: A strong answer sees the same pattern in both: mixing happens by itself, unmixing does not.

items.p: Meera wants to test whether wet waste spoils cotton cloth too. Which test is fair?
opts: Put a cotton rag in sambar and compare it with nothing
Put one cotton rag in a dry jar and the same kind of rag in a jar with sambar, for the same time
Put cotton in sambar and plastic in water
Ask a friend what they think
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here the only difference is the sambar. Without a dry jar to compare, she can't be sure the sambar made the difference.

items.p: Two people talk about the Minamata story.

views.says: The factory should have tested its waste before pouring it into the sea.

views.who: Ramesh, a factory owner in the 1950s
views.says: Nobody knew then that mercury builds up in fish. The sea looked big enough to take anything.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with? Use what you know about how the mercury built up. Then say what the other person gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, explains that mercury built up from tiny living things to small fish to big fish, and fairly admits the other point, for example that it was not well understood at first. It may add that after people fell ill, the factory kept pouring for years.
items.why: This is a real argument about who is responsible when harm is not yet understood. The factory went on pouring waste until 1968, long after the illness was found.

items.p: In the Sorting Race, a child sorted the mixed round faster than the first round. Think of two reasons this might happen.
items.a: They had practised in the first round and knew the things. Or the mixed bowl had too little water, so nothing stuck. Or the first round was handed over slowly.
items.why: Explaining an odd result is real science. A strong answer gives reasons that could be checked, like practice, and suggests a fix, like doing each round twice or swapping the order.
items.context: In the Sorting Race, you timed sorting 30 things as they were handed to you, and then sorting the same 30 after they were mixed with wet tea leaves.

items.p: A building has 40 flats. If one family in every 4 flats sorts badly, how many flats sort badly?
items.why: 40 divided into groups of 4 makes 10 groups. One flat in each group sorts badly, so 10 flats sort badly.

items.p: A city collects sorted waste but takes it all to the same dump. Which change would help most?
opts: Send wet waste to composting and dry waste to recycling centres
items.why: Sorting only helps if each kind goes somewhere that can use it. Burning makes smoke and wastes what could be recycled.

items.p: Draw the path of mercury at Minamata: from the factory, to tiny living things, to small fish, to big fish, to a cat or person. Show the mercury growing at each step.
items.a: A chain of drawings with arrows, from the factory pipe to tiny living things, small fish, big fish and a cat, with more and more dots of mercury at each step.
items.why: The amount grows at each step because each animal eats many of the ones below, and keeps the mercury in their body.

items.p: If a dumping ground is far from your home, its smoke cannot affect you.
items.why: False. In March 2023, smoke from the Brahmapuram dumping ground spread over parts of Kochi for nearly two weeks. Smoke and gases travel on the wind.

items.p: Some people say machines should sort all waste. Name one thing a machine can do well, and one thing no machine can do.
items.a: A magnet can pull out metal quickly. But no machine can take sambar back out of a soaked newspaper.
items.why: A strong answer is fair to machines and also uses the Two-Jar Test to show where they can't help.

items.p: Three of these make sorting easier at home. Which one makes it harder?
opts: Putting the bins right beside the stove
A small bowl for tea leaves near the tea pot
items.why: One bin means everything gets mixed. The others put the right choice close at hand, which makes it easy.

items.p: Why do waste pickers earn more from sorted dry waste than from mixed waste?
opts: Clean, dry paper and plastic can be sold, but soaked and dirty ones can't
items.why: Recyclers pay for clean material they can use. Wet, dirty material is worth little or nothing, and takes hours to clean.

items.p: Plan a new test: does wet waste spoil glass, like it spoils paper? Write your question, what you will compare, and what you predict, with a reason.
items.a: Question: does sambar spoil a glass bottle cap? Compare one glass piece in a dry jar with one in a sambar jar. Predict: the glass will rinse clean, because glass, like plastic, does not soak up liquid.
items.why: A strong plan asks one question, changes only one thing, and gives a prediction with a reason.

items.p: Sort these by what happens when they meet sambar.
cats: Soaks it up and is spoiled
Gets dirty but can be rinsed
items: Soaks it up and is spoiled
Gets dirty but can be rinsed
Soaks it up and is spoiled
Gets dirty but can be rinsed
Soaks it up and is spoiled
Gets dirty but can be rinsed
items.a: see items
items.why: Paper, cardboard and cloth are made of fibres with gaps, so liquid soaks in. Steel, glass and plastic have no such gaps, so liquid stays on the surface.

items.p: A gas made deep in rotting garbage heaps, which warms the Earth and burns easily, is called ____.
items.why: Methane is made when food rots without air. It is also the main gas in the biogas used for cooking in some homes.

items.p: Lissy chechi, a waste collector in a story, said: 'It takes one minute to mix. It takes a person all day to pull a mixed heap apart.' Do your own tests agree with her? Explain.
items.a: Yes. In the Sorting Race, mixing took ten seconds, but sorting the mixed bowl took much longer than sorting as I threw. In the Two-Jar Test, some things could not be unmixed at all.
items.why: A strong answer uses numbers or results from the child's own tests, not only agreement.

experiments.title: The Two-Jar Test: what does wet waste do to dry waste?
experiments.context: This is the Two-Jar Test. You put the same dry waste in two jars, add wet waste to one, and find out what the wet waste does to the dry.
experiments.question: If dry waste is thrown in with wet waste for just 15 minutes, can the dry waste still be sold for recycling? Which kinds survive, and which are spoiled?
experiments.predict: Look at the newspaper, the biscuit-box piece and the milk packet. Which of them do you think will still be good enough for the kabadiwala after sitting in sambar? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both jars get exactly the same dry things, cut to the same size, and wait for the same time. Only one thing is different: one jar also gets wet waste. So any difference must come from the wet waste.

materials.item: 2 clean glass jars or steel dabbas of the same size, with lids
2 strips of newspaper, each about 4 cm wide and as long as a ruler
2 pieces cut from an empty biscuit or cereal box, each about the size of a playing card
2 strips cut from an empty, rinsed milk packet, about the size of a playing card
2 big spoons of leftover sambar, dal or rasam, a spoon of cooked rice, and a banana or onion peel
an old plate or newspaper to work on, a spoon or kitchen tongs, a marker and two labels

experiments.safety: Use a spoon or tongs, or wear gloves, to take things out of the mixed jar. Wash hands with soap afterwards. If you keep the mixed jar overnight, a grown-up opens it near a window and nobody sniffs it closely.

schedule.what: Guess, set up both jars, shake them gently and wait 15 minutes. Then do the lift test, the pull test and the rinse test, and fill in the table.
If you kept the closed jars overnight, a grown-up opens each one near a window. Compare the smell, then empty the mixed jar into the wet bin.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick the dry newspaper strip and a scrap of the soaked one side by side in your notebook once both are dry, and write one sentence about each.

setup.art: Two empty glass jars on a plate, labelled DRY ONLY and MIXED, with matching newspaper strips, biscuit-box pieces and milk packet strips laid in front of each.
setup.caption: 1. Put the same three dry things in front of each jar.

setup.art: A child spooning sambar, rice and a peel into the jar labelled MIXED, on top of the dry things.
setup.caption: 2. Add wet waste to the MIXED jar only.

setup.art: Both jars with lids on, being tipped gently from side to side, and a kitchen timer showing 15 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Close both jars, tip them five times, and wait 15 minutes.

setup.art: A child lifting a soaked orange newspaper strip by one end with tongs as it tears, and beside it a dry strip held up whole.
setup.caption: 4. Lift and gently pull each newspaper strip.

setup.art: A milk packet strip being rinsed under a tap and coming out clean, next to a stained biscuit-box piece that stays orange.
setup.caption: 5. Rinse the milk packet and the biscuit-box piece. Which comes clean?

flow.do: 1. Lay the dry things in two matching sets on a plate. 2. Ask your child to guess which ones will still be sellable after sitting in sambar.
flow.say: We are going to put these in two jars. One jar gets sambar and peels too. Which of these will still be good enough to sell? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the newspaper, the box piece and the milk packet. Which will still be good after sitting in sambar? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will survive?
good: Plastic doesn't soak things up.
Paper gets soggy.
You can wash plastic.
Cardboard is thicker than newspaper.

flow.parent: Write the guesses in the table before you start. Don't explain anything yet. Many children guess that everything can just be washed afterwards.
flow.context: This is the Two-Jar Test. You put the same dry waste in two jars, add wet waste to one, and find out what the wet waste does to the dry.

flow.do: 1. Label one jar DRY ONLY and the other MIXED. 2. Put one newspaper strip, one box piece and one milk packet strip in each jar. 3. Add the sambar, rice and peel to the MIXED jar only.
flow.say: Both jars get the same dry things. Only the MIXED jar gets wet waste. Why do we keep everything else the same?
flow.kid: Put the same three things in each jar. Now add sambar, rice and a peel to the MIXED jar only.

ask.q: Why does the DRY ONLY jar matter?
good: So we can compare.
It shows what the things are like with no wet waste.
Then we know the sambar made the difference.

flow.parent: The DRY ONLY jar is the control. It shows what happens with nothing changed, so any difference in the MIXED jar comes from the wet waste.

flow.do: 1. Close both lids. 2. Tip each jar gently from side to side five times, like a bag being carried. 3. Set a timer for 15 minutes.
flow.say: A garbage bag gets swung and bumped on its way down the stairs. Tipping the jars does the same. Now we wait 15 minutes.
flow.kid: Close both jars. Tip each one gently five times. Now wait 15 minutes.
flow.parent: Use the wait to play a round of the Three Bins Snap game, or to start setting up the sorting station. You can peek through the glass: the newspaper usually darkens within a few minutes.

flow.do: 1. With tongs or a spoon, lift each newspaper strip out by one end. 2. Hold each by both ends and pull gently.
flow.say: Lift the dry strip first, then the strip from the MIXED jar. Now pull each one very gently from both ends. What happens?
flow.kid: Lift out both newspaper strips. Pull each one gently from both ends. What happens?

ask.q: What did you feel when you pulled the soaked strip?
good: It tore straight away.
It was floppy and broke.
The dry one held, the wet one ripped.

flow.parent: The soaked strip usually tears with a very gentle pull, or even when lifted. The dry strip holds. If the soaked strip holds, pull a little harder on both: the soaked one gives way first.

flow.do: 1. Take out the box piece and the milk packet strip from the MIXED jar. 2. Rinse both under the tap for ten seconds. 3. Compare them with the ones from the DRY ONLY jar.
flow.say: Let's try to wash them. Rinse each one for ten seconds. Which one comes clean? Which one stays stained?
flow.kid: Rinse the box piece and the milk packet for ten seconds. Which comes clean?
flow.parent: The milk packet almost always rinses clean, because plastic does not absorb liquid. The box piece stays stained and goes soft, because cardboard is made of paper fibres that soak up the sambar.

check.q: In the Two-Jar Test, the milk packet from the MIXED jar came clean after rinsing, but the newspaper did not. Why?
options: The milk packet was in the jar for less time
Paper soaks up liquid between its fibres, but plastic does not
Sambar only sticks to newspaper ink
The newspaper was thinner, so it was dirtier
check.why: Paper is made of plant fibres with gaps between them, and liquid soaks into the gaps. Plastic has no gaps, so the sambar only sits on top and can be rinsed off. Picking 'less time' is not right, because both were in the jar for the same 15 minutes. That was part of the fair test.

flow.do: Fill in the table together. For each thing, decide: could the kabadiwala take it?
flow.say: Now let's fill in the table. Which things could we still sell? Which are spoiled for good?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Which things could you still sell? Which are spoiled?

chart.title: Made-up example: results from one family's test
chart.note: These are made up, to show what a table can look like. Yours may be different.
rows: Dry jar yes, mixed jar no
Dry jar yes, mixed jar no

flow.do: Ask for a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
flow.say: Tell me what you found. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why does it happen?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw. Then say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Could we ever get the sambar back out of the newspaper?
good: No, it is inside the paper.
Washing makes the paper fall apart.
No, so we should keep them apart from the start.

flow.parent: A strong answer: 'Wet waste spoils paper and cardboard but not plastic. The newspaper tore and the box piece stayed stained, but the milk packet rinsed clean. Paper soaks up liquid. Once it is in, you can't get it out, so we must keep wet and dry apart from the start.'
flow.think: It took one second to mix them. How long would it take to unmix them?

flow.do: 1. Keep both jars closed overnight, if you like. 2. Next day, a grown-up opens each jar near a window. 3. Compare the smell from a little distance. 4. Empty the MIXED jar into the wet bin and wash both jars.
flow.say: Let's open the jars near the window. Don't put your nose close. Just notice the smell from here. Which jar smells?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to open the jars by the window. Don't sniff closely. Which jar smells?
flow.parent: In a warm room the MIXED jar smells sour after a day, and the newspaper may show spots of mould. The DRY ONLY jar smells of nothing. This is why a bag of mixed waste smells and draws flies, while a box of dry waste does not.

experiments.title: The Sorting Race: sort as you throw, or sort later?
experiments.context: This is the Sorting Race. You time how long it takes to sort 30 things as you throw them, and how long to sort the same 30 things after they are mixed.
experiments.question: How much longer does it take to sort waste after it has been mixed, compared with sorting each thing as you throw it?
experiments.predict: Guess how many seconds each round will take. Will the mixed round take a little longer, twice as long, or much longer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same 30 things, the same three bowls and the same person sorting in both rounds. Only one thing changes: whether the things are mixed first. Do each round twice and take the faster time, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 10 small dry paper things: bits of newspaper, bus tickets, a paper cup, torn notebook pages
10 small plastic or metal things: bottle caps, rinsed milk packet strips, a toothpaste cap, a steel lid
10 small wet things: onion peels, a spoon of used tea leaves, eggshells, a few curry leaves, a banana peel cut in pieces
3 bowls or boxes labelled WET, PAPER and PLASTIC AND METAL, one big bowl for mixing, gloves or a spoon
a phone or clock that shows seconds

experiments.safety: Wear gloves or use a spoon for the mixed round. Wash hands with soap afterwards.
experiments.record: Write your times in the table. Then draw two bars, one for each round, as tall as the faster time.

setup.art: A parent handing a child one bottle cap at a time, while the child drops it into one of three labelled bowls and a phone timer runs.
setup.caption: 1. Round 1: sort each thing as it is handed to you.

setup.art: All 30 things tipped into one big bowl with damp tea leaves, being stirred with a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Put everything back, add a spoon of water, and stir.

setup.art: A child with gloves on picking tea leaves off a scrap of paper over the three bowls, the timer running.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: sort the mixed bowl, and time it.

flow.do: 1. Show the 30 things and the three labelled bowls. 2. Ask for a guess for each round, and a reason.
flow.say: First you will sort these one at a time, as I hand them to you. Then we mix them all and you sort them again. How long will each round take? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how long each round will take. Will the mixed round be slower? Why?

ask.q: Why might the mixed round be slower?
good: You have to search for each thing.
Tea leaves stick to the paper.
Things get stuck together.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Sorting Race. You time sorting before and after mixing.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Hand your child the 30 things one by one, in any order. 3. Stop the timer when the last one is in a bowl. 4. Do it once more and write both times.
flow.say: Ready? I'll hand you one thing at a time. Drop it in the right bowl as fast as you can.
flow.kid: Take each thing and drop it in the right bowl. Go fast!
flow.parent: Round 1 usually takes under a minute. This is what sorting at the bin feels like.

flow.do: 1. Tip everything into the big bowl. 2. Add one spoon of water. 3. Stir well with a spoon for ten seconds.
flow.say: Now we mix it all, the way a single dustbin does. A spoon of water is like the juice from leftovers.
flow.kid: Tip it all in the big bowl. Add a spoon of water. Stir.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts on gloves. 2. Start the timer. 3. They sort the mixed bowl into the three bowls, picking tea leaves off the paper too. 4. Stop when everything is sorted. 5. Do it once more if they want to.
flow.say: Now sort the mixed bowl into the three bowls. Tea leaves stuck to paper count as wet. Pick them off first.
flow.kid: Put on gloves. Sort the mixed bowl into the three bowls. Pick off stuck tea leaves.
flow.parent: The mixed round usually takes several times longer. Used tea leaves stick to damp paper and are fiddly to pick off. Some scraps of paper will be too soggy to save. That is a real result too.

flow.do: 1. Check each bowl for mistakes and count them. 2. Fill in the table. 3. Draw the two bars.
flow.say: Let's check the bowls. Did anything end up in the wrong place? How many times longer did the mixed round take?
flow.kid: Check each bowl. Count the mistakes. Which round was slower? By how much?

check.q: In the Sorting Race, Round 2 took much longer than Round 1. What made it slower?
options: The things were heavier the second time
The things were mixed and stuck together, so each had to be found and pulled apart
check.why: In Round 1 each thing came on its own, so sorting took one quick look. In Round 2 they were mixed, and wet tea leaves stuck to the paper, so each thing had to be searched for and cleaned off. Picking 'tired' is worth checking: that is why we did each round twice.

flow.do: Ask what this means for the dustbin at home.
flow.say: If a whole city's waste comes mixed, how long would sorting take? Who would do it?
flow.kid: Think of a whole city's waste, all mixed. Who would sort it? How long would it take?

ask.q: What is the quickest way to get waste sorted?
good: Sort it when you throw it.
Have two bins at home.
Never mix it in the first place.

experiments.title: Lid or No Lid: who finds the open bin?
experiments.context: This is the Lid or No Lid test. You leave wet waste in an open box and a closed box, and find out which one ants, flies and smells reach.
experiments.question: Does a lid really keep ants, flies and smells away from wet waste?
experiments.predict: Which box do you think ants or flies will find first? Will they reach the closed box at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both boxes get the same waste and stand side by side in the same spot for the same time. The only difference is the lid.

materials.item: 2 small boxes or katoris of the same size, one with a tight lid
2 pieces of banana peel, each with a few drops of jaggery water or a little sugar on it
a spot on the kitchen counter or balcony floor where you have seen ants

experiments.safety: Wash hands after touching the peels. Throw both peels into the wet bin when you finish.

schedule.what: Set up both boxes side by side. Check and count after 1 hour and after 4 hours.
Check and count the next morning. Open the closed box and look inside. Empty both into the wet bin.

experiments.record: Write your counts in the table at each check. Draw both boxes on day 2.

setup.art: Two small steel katoris side by side on a kitchen counter, each holding a piece of banana peel, one with its lid on.
setup.caption: 1. Put the same peel in two boxes. Close one.

setup.art: A line of ants walking to the open katori, and a child kneeling to count them with a pencil and notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Check after 1 hour, 4 hours and the next morning. Count ants and flies.

flow.do: Show both boxes and ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Both boxes get a sweet peel. One has a lid. Who will find the peels? Will anyone get into the closed box? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which box will ants or flies find? Can they get in the closed one? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lid or No Lid test. You find out whether a lid keeps creatures away from wet waste.

flow.do: 1. Put one peel in each box. 2. Close one box tightly. 3. Put both side by side where you have seen ants.
flow.say: We put them right next to each other. Then the place is the same for both, and only the lid is different.
flow.kid: Put a peel in each box. Close one. Put them side by side.

flow.do: Check after 1 hour and after 4 hours. Count the ants and flies on or around each box.
flow.say: Let's look. How many ants? Any flies? Where are they going?
flow.kid: Count the ants and flies at each box. Write the numbers.
flow.wait: Check after 1 hour and after 4 hours.
flow.parent: In a warm Indian kitchen, ants usually find the open peel within a few hours. Ants follow smell trails, and they lay new trails for other ants. If no ants come, look for tiny fruit flies by the next morning. If nothing at all comes, leave the boxes one more day.

flow.do: 1. Next morning, count again. 2. Open the closed box and look inside. 3. Empty both peels into the wet bin and wash the boxes.
flow.say: What did the lid do? Now think of the dustbin under our sink.
flow.kid: Count again. Open the closed box. Did anyone get in?

check.q: In the Lid or No Lid test, ants came to the open box but not to the closed one. What does that tell us about a kitchen bin?
options: A lid keeps the smell in, so ants and flies don't find the waste or get to it
The closed peel had gone bad
check.why: Ants and flies find food by smell. A tight lid keeps most of the smell in and blocks the way in. Picking 'ants only like bananas' is a good thought to test: try a different peel next time and see if the result changes.

activities.title: Set Up a Sorting Station at Home
activities.context: This is the Sorting Station activity. You set up three containers in the kitchen, one for each kind of waste, and label them so everyone at home can use them.

materials.item: a bucket or bin with a lid for wet waste, such as an old paint bucket or a steel dabba
a cardboard box or a cloth bag for dry waste
a small tin, jar or box with a lid for dangerous waste
paper, crayons, a marker and tape

activities.safety: Do not handle any broken glass or blades yourself. Leave them for a grown-up to wrap.
activities.record: Draw your sorting station, with an arrow from three things you threw out today to the right container.

setup.art: A kitchen corner under the sink with a lidded steel bucket marked WET, a cardboard box marked DRY and a small tin with a red cross.
setup.caption: 1. Put three containers in one place, close to where waste is made.

setup.art: A child drawing pictures of a peel, a milk packet and a battery on three paper labels, and taping them on.
setup.caption: 2. Make a picture label for each one, so even small children can use it.

flow.do: Look at where waste is thrown in your home now. Ask your child how many bins there are and what goes in each.
flow.say: Where do we throw things at home? Is there one bin, or more? Let's make a station with three.
flow.kid: Look at your home's dustbins. How many are there? What goes in each?
flow.context: This is the first step of setting up a sorting station at home.

flow.do: 1. Put the wet bin, the dry box and the danger tin side by side, close to where you cook. 2. Put the danger tin up high, out of small children's reach.
flow.say: We keep them together near the stove. Then sorting takes no extra walking. Why should the danger tin go up high?
flow.kid: Put the three together near the kitchen. Put the danger tin up high.

ask.q: Why put all three together, close to the stove?
good: So it is easy to sort.
So nobody is lazy and uses the wrong one.
Because that is where most waste is made.

flow.do: Your child writes WET, DRY and DANGER, and draws three examples on each label. Tape the labels on.
flow.say: Draw three things for each label, so even someone who can't read knows what goes where.
flow.kid: Write WET, DRY and DANGER. Draw three things on each label. Tape them on.
flow.parent: Good pictures: peels, tea leaves and eggshells for WET. Newspaper, a milk packet and a bottle for DRY. A battery, a tube light and tablets for DANGER.

flow.do: Show the station to everyone at home and agree to try it for a week.
flow.say: Let's show everyone. Rinse packets before they go in DRY. Wrap broken glass before it goes anywhere.
flow.kid: Show your family the station. Teach them where each thing goes.

check.q: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, has just finished a cup of curd. Where should the empty plastic curd cup go?
options: In the wet bin, because it had curd in it
Rinse it, then put it in the dry box
check.why: The cup is plastic, so it is dry waste. A quick rinse stops the leftover curd from spoiling the paper in the dry box. Picking 'wet bin' is a common mistake: the curd was wet, but the cup will not rot.

activities.title: Sorting Week: a tally of mistakes
activities.context: This is the Sorting Week activity. For seven days you check the bins at home once a day and make a tally mark for each thing in the wrong place.

materials.item: a tally sheet stuck on the wall by the bins, with a pencil on a string
a spoon or gloves for moving things that are in the wrong bin

activities.safety: Use a spoon or gloves to move things. Never move broken glass. Call a grown-up. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Make the tally sheet with one row for each day. Check the bins in the evening and tally the mistakes.
Check and tally. Count up each day's marks and see whether the mistakes went down.

activities.record: The tally sheet, with the total for each day, and one sentence about the most common mistake.

setup.art: A sheet on the kitchen wall with seven rows for the days and a column for tally marks, a pencil hanging from a string.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a tally sheet beside the bins.

setup.art: A child peeking into the dry box with a spoon and finding a tea bag, then making a tally mark.
setup.caption: 2. Each evening, look in each bin and make a mark for each thing in the wrong place.

flow.do: Make a sheet with seven rows, Monday to Sunday. Show your child how a tally works: four lines, then a fifth across them.
flow.say: Every evening you are the bin inspector. For each thing in the wrong bin, make one mark.
flow.kid: You are the bin inspector. Each evening, make one mark for each thing in the wrong bin.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sorting Week. You check the bins every evening for a week.

flow.do: Each evening, your child looks in each bin with a spoon. They move anything in the wrong place and make a mark.
flow.say: What did you find today? Who do you think put it there? Let's not blame anyone. Let's just fix it.
flow.kid: Look in each bin with a spoon. Move anything in the wrong place. Make a mark.
flow.wait: Do this every evening for seven days.
flow.parent: Common mistakes: tea bags and wet tissues in the dry box, unrinsed packets, and plastic bags of peels in the wet bin. Plastic should not go in the wet bin, because it will not rot.

flow.do: On day 7, count each day's marks. Draw a bar chart with seven bars.
flow.say: Did the mistakes go up or down through the week? What was the most common one?
flow.kid: Count the marks for each day. Did they go down? Which mistake happened most?

check.q: In Sorting Week, Meenakshi found tea bags in the dry box on four days. What is the best fix?
options: Put a small bowl for tea bags right beside the stove, and empty it into the wet bin
check.why: Most sorting mistakes happen because the right bin is not close at hand. Making the right choice the easy choice fixes it. Tea bags are wet waste, though some have a little plastic in them, so check yours.

activities.title: The Danger Box: find and wrap hazardous waste
activities.context: This is the Danger Box activity. With a grown-up, you look around your home for dangerous waste and pack it safely, so it cannot hurt the people who collect it.

materials.item: a box or tin with a lid, marked with a red cross
old newspapers, tape and a marker

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the touching and wrapping of glass, blades, tube lights, batteries and medicines. The child points, names and labels. Never open a battery or break a tube light.
activities.record: Make a list of the dangerous things you found, and next to each, write why it is dangerous.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child looking in a kitchen drawer and finding old batteries and a strip of expired tablets.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt with a grown-up for dangerous waste at home.

setup.art: A grown-up wrapping a used razor blade in thick newspaper, while the child writes SHARP on it.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up wraps it. You write what it is on the wrapping.

flow.do: Explain what hazardous waste is. Ask your child to guess three things at home that might be dangerous to throw out.
flow.say: Some waste can cut, poison or catch fire. Can you think of three things at home like that?
flow.kid: Some waste can cut, poison or catch fire. Can you think of three?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Danger Box activity. You hunt for dangerous waste at home with a grown-up.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen, bathroom and drawers together. Your child points, and you pick up anything dangerous.
flow.say: Point to anything you think is dangerous. I will pick it up. What makes it dangerous?
flow.kid: Point to dangerous waste. Let the grown-up pick it up. Say why it is dangerous.

ask.q: Why is a broken tube light dangerous?
good: It has sharp glass.
It has mercury inside, a poison.
It can cut someone.

flow.parent: Look for used batteries, dead phone batteries, a fused tube light or CFL bulb, expired medicines, used blades, broken glass, old paint or mosquito-repellent refills. Keep phone batteries away from heat. Don't break tube lights, and wrap them whole.

flow.do: 1. Wrap glass and blades in thick newspaper. 2. Your child writes on each packet what is inside. 3. Put batteries, medicines and bulbs in the box.
flow.say: Write on each packet in big letters, like BROKEN GLASS or SHARP. Then the person who picks it up knows to be careful.
flow.kid: Write on each packet in big letters. BROKEN GLASS. SHARP. Then the collector knows.
flow.parent: Ask your building, your city's waste helpline, or a shop that sells batteries or bulbs where to take the danger box. Many cities have collection days or points for this.

check.q: Why should old medicines never be flushed down the toilet?
options: They can get into rivers and the sea and harm fish and other animals
They will make the toilet smell
check.why: Toilet water goes to drains and, often, to rivers. Many medicines are not removed by water treatment, so they reach fish and other water animals. Keep them in the danger box instead.

activities.title: Clean and Safe Walk around the building
activities.context: This is the Clean and Safe Walk. If you can walk around your building or lane with a grown-up, you look for places where waste makes things unsafe, and for places kept clean.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil, or a phone to take photos

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Don't touch any waste, and keep away from stray animals at garbage heaps.
activities.record: Make a tally of what you saw: open bins, closed bins, litter, still water, blocked drains. Write one thing your building could do better.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up walking round an apartment building's ground floor with a notebook, pointing at an overflowing bin.
setup.caption: 1. Walk around your building or lane with a grown-up.

setup.art: A child crouching to look at a coconut shell with rainwater in it, and drawing a tally mark in the notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Tally what you see: open bins, litter, still water, blocked drains.

flow.do: Before you go, make a tally sheet with five rows: open bins, closed bins, litter, still water, blocked drains.
flow.say: We are going to be safety inspectors. What could make our building unsafe?
flow.kid: Make five rows: open bins, closed bins, litter, still water, blocked drains.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clean and Safe Walk. Do this only if you can go round your building or lane with a grown-up.

flow.do: Walk around the building, the parking area and the gate. Your child makes a tally mark for each thing they see.
flow.say: Look for anything that holds still water: cups, tyres, pots, coconut shells. Mosquitoes can breed in them.
flow.kid: Look carefully. Make a mark for each thing you see. Look for still water.
flow.parent: If you can't go out, do this from a window or balcony, or around your own flat. Look at pots, buckets, the fridge tray and plant saucers too.

flow.do: Count the tallies at home and talk about one change your building could make.
flow.say: What was the biggest problem? What could we ask the building to change?
flow.kid: Count your marks. What was the biggest problem? What one change would help?

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, finds a coconut shell full of rainwater near her building's gate. Why should it be emptied?
options: Mosquitoes can lay eggs in still water, and some spread dengue
check.why: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water, and the young grow there for about a week. Some kinds spread dengue. Emptying the shell and turning it upside down stops this. 'It looks untidy' is true, but it is not the main danger.

projects.title: A Picture Sorting Guide for Our Building
projects.context: This is the Sorting Guide project. Over three days you make a picture poster that shows 18 everyday things and which bin each one goes in, for your family or your building.

materials.item: a large sheet of chart paper, or four A4 sheets taped together
crayons or sketch pens, a ruler, glue, and old newspaper or magazine pictures to cut out

projects.safety: A grown-up asks the building's office or secretary before the poster goes up in a shared place.

schedule.what: List 18 things your family throws out, and sort them on paper into WET, DRY and DANGER. Check any tricky ones.
Draw the three columns on the chart paper. Draw or stick a picture of each thing in the right column.
Add the three golden rules at the bottom. Show it to your family and ask one neighbour what they think.

projects.record: A photo of the finished poster, and one thing a neighbour or family member said about it.

setup.art: A child at a table with a list of things sorted into three columns on a notebook page.
setup.caption: 1. Make a list of 18 things and sort them.

setup.art: A large poster with three coloured columns, WET in green, DRY in blue and DANGER with a red cross, filled with drawings.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each thing in its column on a big sheet.

setup.art: The finished poster taped beside a building's lift, with a neighbour reading it.
setup.caption: 3. Add three rules at the bottom and share it.

flow.do: 1. Together, list 18 things your family throws out. 2. Sort them into WET, DRY and DANGER. 3. Put a question mark next to any tricky ones and talk them over.
flow.say: What do we throw out most? Let's list 18 things. Which ones are tricky?
flow.kid: List 18 things your family throws out. Sort them into WET, DRY and DANGER.
flow.parent: Tricky ones: a used tissue, a chips packet, a pizza box with cheese, a tea bag, a broken toy, an old toothbrush, a used diaper. Tissues and stained food boxes are often taken as wet or reject waste. Check your city's rules. Chips packets are dry waste, but many recyclers don't take them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sorting Guide project. You list and sort 18 things your family throws out.

flow.do: 1. Draw three columns on the chart paper. 2. Colour the headings green, blue and red. 3. Draw or stick six things in each column.
flow.say: Make the pictures big. Someone walking past should understand it without reading.
flow.kid: Draw three columns. Draw six things in each. Make them big.

flow.do: 1. Write three rules at the bottom. 2. Show it to your family. 3. If the building agrees, put it up near the bins or the lift.
flow.say: What are the three most important rules? Let's write them at the bottom.
flow.kid: Write three rules at the bottom. Show your family. Ask a neighbour what they think.
flow.parent: Good rules: 'Sort it when you throw it.' 'Rinse packets before they go in DRY.' 'Wrap and mark broken glass.'

check.q: Which rule would save the most dry waste from being spoiled?
options: Keep wet waste out of the dry bin
Take the waste out once a week
check.why: Wet waste soaks into paper and cardboard and spoils them for good, as the Two-Jar Test showed. Keeping them apart saves the dry waste. Taking waste out only once a week would make wet waste smell and draw flies.

challenges.title: A Bin That Fits a Small Kitchen
challenges.context: This is the Small Kitchen Bin challenge. Many city flats have tiny kitchens. You design and build a sorting bin that fits in a small space.
challenges.problem: Design a bin for a small flat kitchen that keeps wet and dry waste apart, keeps smells and ants out, and fits in the space under the sink or beside the stove.
constraints: It must fit in a space about as big as a school bag.
Wet waste must have a lid.
It must be easy to empty and clean.
Use only things already in your home.
materials: old plastic or steel containers with lids
general: Two containers side by side: a lidded bucket for wet waste and a box for dry waste.
A bin with two parts inside, made by fixing a cardboard wall down the middle.
Stacking: a small lidded wet bin on top of a flat dry box.
creative: Hang a cloth bag for dry waste on the inside of the cupboard door, so it uses no floor space.
Fix a small steel dabba to the wall beside the stove for tea leaves and peels, emptied into the wet bin every evening.
Make the dry box from a big cardboard box with a slot on top, like a post box, so only flat dry things go in.
challenges.your_turn: Measure the space in your kitchen. Draw your bin design with measurements, build a model or the real thing, and use it for three days. What would you change?

setup.art: A child measuring the gap beside a kitchen stove with a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the space you have.

setup.art: A cardboard box divided in two by a cardboard wall, with a lid on one half, labelled WET and DRY.
setup.caption: 2. Build your design from things at home.

flow.do: Measure the space in your kitchen with a ruler.
flow.say: Where is there room for a bin? Let's measure it.
flow.kid: Find a space for the bin. Measure how wide and how tall it is.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Small Kitchen Bin challenge.

flow.do: Draw a design, with the measurements written on it.
flow.say: Draw your bin. Show where wet goes and where dry goes. How will you keep smells in?
flow.kid: Draw your bin. Show where wet and dry waste go. Add a lid.

flow.do: Build it from cardboard and old containers.
flow.say: Let's build it. Does it fit? Does the lid close?
flow.kid: Build your bin. Check that it fits and the lid closes.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together. Compare them with yours.
flow.say: Here are some other ideas. Which one would you borrow?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Which one would you add to yours?

check.q: In the Small Kitchen Bin challenge, why must the wet part have a lid?
options: To keep smells in and keep ants and flies out
So the dry waste can't be seen
check.why: Wet waste smells as it rots, and the smell draws ants and flies. The Lid or No Lid test showed that a lid keeps them away.

challenges.title: An Onam Sadya with No Mixed Waste
challenges.context: This is the Festival Feast challenge. Big feasts make a lot of waste quickly. You plan how to keep it sorted.
challenges.problem: Your family is serving an Onam sadya, a Kerala feast eaten on banana leaves, to 20 guests at home. Plan how to sort every bit of waste so that nothing ends up mixed.
constraints: Guests should not have to think hard about where to throw things.
No waste may be left lying in the open.
Plan for leaves, leftover food, water bottles, paper napkins and anything broken.
materials: paper and crayons for the plan
the bins and boxes you have at home
general: Put a big labelled wet bin right where people finish eating, for banana leaves and leftovers.
Serve water in steel tumblers instead of plastic bottles.
Have one person stand by the bins at the end to help guests.
creative: Ask each guest to fold their banana leaf and carry it to the wet bin themselves, as many families do.
Use cloth napkins that are washed afterwards, so there is no paper to soak.
Make a picture sign at the door showing the three bins, drawn by the children.
challenges.your_turn: Draw a plan of your home on feast day. Mark where each bin goes and who looks after it. Then use it at your next family festival or party, and check the bins afterwards.

setup.art: A long row of guests seated on the floor eating a sadya on banana leaves, with a green bin at the end of the row.
setup.caption: 1. Picture the feast and all its waste.

setup.art: A child's drawn floor plan of a flat with a green bin, a blue box and a red-cross box marked in place.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a plan showing where each bin goes.

flow.do: List all the waste a feast for 20 guests makes.
flow.say: What will be left after 20 people eat? Let's make a list.
flow.kid: List all the waste a big feast makes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Festival Feast challenge.

flow.do: Draw a plan of the home, marking each bin and who looks after it.
flow.say: Where do people eat? Where will they throw things? Put the bins where they are needed.
flow.kid: Draw your home. Mark where each bin goes. Who helps the guests?

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions. Add the best ideas to your plan.
flow.say: Here are other ideas. Which would work in our home?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Add one to your plan.

check.q: At the Onam sadya, where should the used banana leaves go?
options: In the wet bin, because leaves rot and can be composted
check.why: Banana leaves are part of a plant, so tiny living things in soil feed on them and they rot. That makes them wet waste, and good for compost. Burning them makes smoke that harms the lungs.

videos.title: Revolutionising Waste Management and Recycling in India: Hasiru Dala Innovations
videos.why: Shows waste pickers in Bengaluru sorting dry waste by kind at a collection centre. It shows where a sorted blue bag really goes, and why clean dry waste matters.
videos.check: Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's public title lookup. A parent should preview it. Its length is a guess.

videos.title: Bin Boy
videos.why: A short film made to persuade Indian families to sort wet, dry and hazardous waste every day. A boy sits in a dustbin until his family listens. Good for talking about whose job sorting is.
videos.check: Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's public title lookup, and described in news reports from March 2022. It was made by a company as a public message. A parent should preview it. Its length is a guess.

videos.title: The 'Dancing Cat' Disaster of Japan: Minamata Explained
videos.why: For the parent first. Explains how mercury from a factory built up in fish at Minamata, which goes with the how-we-found-out card and the danger box.
videos.check: Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's public title lookup. It talks about illness and death, so a parent should watch it first and decide whether to show it. Its length is a guess.

quiz.p: Which of these is wet waste?
opts: Used coffee powder from the filter
quiz.why: Coffee powder comes from a plant and rots. That makes it wet waste. Picking 'milk packet' is a common mistake because milk is wet, but the packet is plastic and does not rot.

quiz.p: Which one goes in the danger box?
quiz.why: Phone batteries can catch fire if they are crushed in a truck. The others are ordinary wet or dry waste.

quiz.p: Sneha, a girl in Class 3, puts a newspaper strip in a jar of dal for 15 minutes, and another strip in an empty jar. What will she most likely find?
opts: The strip in the dal is soaked and tears easily
The strip in the empty jar tears
quiz.why: Paper soaks up liquid between its fibres, so the dal strip weakens and tears. The strip in the empty jar is the comparison, and it stays strong.

quiz.p: In the Two-Jar Test, why did we also have a jar with no sambar?
opts: To compare, so we know the sambar caused the difference
To keep the newspaper for later
quiz.why: The jar with no sambar shows what happens when nothing is changed. Then any difference in the other jar must come from the sambar.

quiz.p: When is it easiest to sort waste?
opts: When you throw each thing, before anything is mixed
quiz.why: Before mixing, each thing takes one second to place. After mixing, things stick together and some, like soaked paper, can never be saved.

quiz.p: In the Sorting Race, sorting the mixed bowl took much longer. What was the main reason?
opts: Things were stuck together and had to be found and pulled apart
There were more things in Round 2
quiz.why: Both rounds had the same 30 things. In Round 2 they were mixed, and wet tea leaves stuck to the paper. Unmixing takes work.

quiz.p: Why should a fused tube light be kept whole and not broken?
opts: It holds a tiny amount of mercury, a poison, and sharp glass
It is worth a lot of money
quiz.why: Kept whole, the mercury stays sealed inside and the glass cuts nobody. Wrap it and keep it in the danger box.

quiz.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and their young grow there for about a week. Some mosquitoes spread dengue.

quiz.why: Ants and flies find food by smell. A lid keeps most of the smell in and blocks the way in.

quiz.p: How does sorting at home help the woman who collects your waste?
opts: She is not cut by hidden glass, and she can sell clean dry waste
It means she doesn't need gloves
quiz.why: Wrapped glass is safe to handle, and clean paper and plastic can be sold. Gloves are still needed.

quiz.p: At Minamata in Japan, a factory poured mercury into the sea. What happened to it?
opts: It spread out and became harmless
It built up in fish, and people and cats who ate them were poisoned
It sank and stayed in the factory pipe
quiz.why: Tiny living things took up the mercury, small fish ate them and big fish ate many small fish. So the poison built up. This is why poisonous waste is kept apart.

quiz.p: Which of these can be rinsed and still go in the dry bin?
opts: A curd cup with curd on it
A paper plate covered in oil
quiz.why: Plastic does not absorb liquid, so a rinsed curd cup is clean dry waste. Paper and cardboard soak up food and oil, so they can't be saved.

applications: Cities like Indore and Mysuru collect waste already sorted, and turn wet waste into compost and dry waste into recycled material.
Dry waste collection centres, many run by waste pickers, sort paper, plastic, metal and glass by kind and sell them to recyclers.
Biogas plants use sorted wet waste to make cooking gas.
Apartment buildings compost their own wet waste and use it on their gardens and potted plants.
Hospitals sort their waste into coloured bins, so sharp and infected things are handled safely.
Festivals and weddings that plan their bins send far less to dumping grounds.
Mosquito control: clearing thrown-away containers that hold water is one of the main ways cities fight dengue.
Battery and bulb collection points keep mercury and other harmful metals out of soil and water.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to get every family in a city to sort their waste?
open_questions.why_open: Cities have tried fines, rewards, school campaigns, and refusing to collect mixed bags. What works in one city often fails in another, and people still argue about why.

open_questions.q: Should cities sort waste at home, in big machine plants, or both?
open_questions.why_open: Machines are getting better at sorting dry waste, but they are costly and can take work away from waste pickers. No one agrees on the best mix.

open_questions.q: How harmful are the tiny amounts of mercury and other metals from old batteries and bulbs that reach dumps?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure them in soil and water near some dumps, but it is hard to say how much harm they do over many years.

open_questions.q: Can we make packets that are easy to sort and recycle, like chips packets?
open_questions.why_open: Many packets are made of several layers stuck together, like plastic and metal foil. Pulling the layers apart is hard, and researchers are still working on it.

maths.problem: In the Sorting Race, Round 1 took 45 seconds. Round 2, with mixed waste, took 3 times as long. How long did Round 2 take?
maths.answer: 135 seconds, which is 2 minutes and 15 seconds.
maths.explain: 3 times 45 is 45 + 45 + 45. 45 + 45 is 90, and 90 + 45 is 135. So Round 2 took 135 seconds. 120 seconds is 2 minutes, and 15 seconds are left over.
maths.context: In the Sorting Race, you time sorting 30 things as they are handed to you, then sorting the same 30 after they are mixed.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'mixed waste is slower' is a start. Multiplying shows exactly how much more time mixing costs.

maths.problem: In Sorting Week, Kavya made these tallies of mistakes: Monday 8, Tuesday 6, Wednesday 6, Thursday 4, Friday 3, Saturday 2, Sunday 1. Did the mistakes go down? On which day did they first go below half of Monday's?
maths.answer: Yes, they went down. Half of Monday's 8 is 4. Thursday had exactly 4, so Friday, with 3, was the first day below half.
maths.explain: Each day had the same or fewer mistakes than the day before, so they went down. Half of 8 is 4. 4 is not below 4, so Thursday doesn't count. Friday's 3 is below 4.
maths.context: In Sorting Week, you check the bins every evening for seven days and make a tally mark for each thing in the wrong bin.

chart.title: Made-up example: sorting mistakes each day

maths.why_maths: A tally turns a feeling, 'we're getting better', into evidence you can check.

maths.problem: A collector buys clean, dry newspaper for 12 rupees a kilogram. A family has 5 kilograms of clean newspaper and 2 kilograms that got soaked in curry. How much money does the family get?
maths.explain: Only the clean newspaper can be sold. 5 kilograms times 12 rupees is 60 rupees. The 2 soaked kilograms are worth nothing, so they would have earned 24 more rupees if they had been kept dry.
maths.context: In the Two-Jar Test, you found that newspaper soaked in sambar tears and can't be recycled. Collectors only buy clean, dry paper. The price here is made up.
maths.why_maths: Working out the money shows that mixing has a real cost, paid by someone.

maths.problem: A building has 48 flats. A waste collector can collect from 8 flats in 10 minutes if the waste is sorted. How long does she take for the whole building?
maths.explain: 48 flats in groups of 8 makes 6 groups, because 6 times 8 is 48. Each group takes 10 minutes. 6 times 10 is 60 minutes.
maths.context: Waste collectors go from flat to flat collecting bags of sorted waste. The numbers here are made up.
maths.why_maths: Grouping lets you plan a big job by thinking about one small part of it.

maths.problem: In the Lid or No Lid test, Divya counted 14 ants at the open box after 4 hours and 0 at the closed box. The next morning there were 23 at the open box. How many more ants came overnight?
maths.explain: 23 take away 14 is 9. You can check: 14 + 9 = 23. More ants came because ants that find food lay a smell trail that leads other ants to it.
maths.context: In the Lid or No Lid test, you leave a sweet banana peel in an open box and in a closed box, and count the ants at each.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows that the ants kept coming, which tells us something about how they find food.

roots.context: We have been learning to sort waste, and finding out that mixing is quick and unmixing is slow. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the mixed jar, sambar soaked into the newspaper by itself within minutes. Once soaked, the paper tore when lifted and could not be sold. Mixing took no effort, but no rinsing could undo it. So the easiest moment to sort waste is the moment you throw it.
deep_truth.habit: We think of sorting as a job for someone later: the truck, the waste picker, the plant. But mixing starts the moment things touch, and undoing it is slow, dirty work. So sorting belongs to the person holding the waste.
deep_truth.evidence: In the two-jar test, the dry newspaper stayed whole while the one beside the sambar soaked and tore. In the sorting race, sorting the mixed heap took several times longer than sorting as you threw. Waste pickers at dumping grounds spend whole days pulling dry waste out of mixed heaps.

three.who_am_i: You are the person holding the waste at the one moment when sorting is easy. That makes you the first part of the city's cleaning.
three.what_is_life: Living things in nature mostly keep their leftovers where others can use them. A fallen leaf feeds worms and fungi right where it falls.
three.what_is_this_world: A world where things mix by themselves and only work can pull them apart. Every clean street is kept clean by someone's work.

roots.thread: In nature, one living thing's leftovers become another's food, because they stay where others can reach them. A leaf falls and is eaten by worms and fungi, and the soil they make feeds the tree. People's waste breaks this circle when it is mixed. A peel stuck in plastic cannot feed the soil, and paper soaked in curry cannot become paper again. Sorting puts each thing back where it can be used.

teachings.teaching: Deal with a hard thing while it is still easy. Handle a great thing while it is still small.
teachings.link: Sorting one peel at the bin takes a second. Sorting a mountain of mixed waste takes years, and may never be done.

teachings.teaching: Water makes the outside clean. Truthfulness makes the inside clean.
teachings.link: In the two-jar test, water rinsed the milk packet clean, but it could not clean the soaked paper. Water cleans only the outside of things.

teachings.source: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography (The Story of My Experiments with Truth), 1927
teachings.teaching: Gandhi insisted that everyone in his home and ashram clean up their own waste, including the toilets. In India this work was often forced onto people of certain castes.
teachings.link: Taking charge of our own waste means not leaving the dirty and dangerous part to someone else.

science.text: Things that are mixed tend to stay mixed, and separating them takes energy. Physicists measure how mixed-up things are with a quantity called entropy, and left to itself it does not go down.
Some poisons, like mercury, build up as they pass from small living things to the animals that eat them. Big fish can hold far more mercury than the water around them.

other_view.view: Asking every family to sort is unreliable, and families make many mistakes. It is better to collect waste and sort it in big plants with machines and trained, well-paid workers. This is an honest view, and some cities do both.

practice.title: The bin pause

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1950s, people living around Minamata Bay in Japan began to fall ill. Their hands shook, they stumbled, and some could not speak clearly. Cats in fishing families twitched and fell, and birds dropped from the sky. A chemical factory had been pouring its waste water into the bay since the 1930s. Many people believed the sea was so big that any waste poured in would spread out and become harmless. In 1956, Hajime Hosokawa, a doctor at the factory's own hospital, reported the illness to health officials. In 1959, scientists at Kumamoto University found the cause: a poisonous form of mercury from the factory. Tiny living things in the water had taken it up. Small fish ate them, and big fish ate many small fish, so the mercury built up instead of spreading out. People and cats who ate the fish were poisoned. That same year, Hosokawa fed the factory's waste water to cats, and one became ill in the same way. The company kept his result quiet. The government only accepted the cause in 1968. Writers like Michiko Ishimure helped the world hear the families' story.
how_we_found_out.who: Hajime Hosokawa, a doctor, the research team at Kumamoto University, and the writer Michiko Ishimure, who told the families' story
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That poisonous waste poured into the huge sea would spread out and become harmless. Instead, the mercury built up in fish, and the people and cats who ate them were poisoned.
how_we_found_out.art: A quiet fishing bay in Japan in the 1950s, small wooden boats on the water, a factory chimney on the shore, and a doctor in a white coat kneeling beside a cat on a jetty.
